items.title: `nx add` silently drops extra arguments instead of forwarding them to the plugin's `init` generator (regression since 20.5.0)
items.body:
### Current Behavior

Arguments passed to `nx add` after the package specifier are accepted without error but never reach the plugin's `init` generator. For example:

```shell
nx add @nx/js --formatter=prettier
```

runs `@nx/js:init` with its defaults (`formatter: none`); `--formatter=prettier` is ignored without any warning.

The CLI still collects the arguments: `add/command-object.ts` sets `unknown-options-as-args: true` and calls `withOverrides(args)`, so they end up in `AddOptions.__overrides_unparsed__`. But nothing reads that field anymore. `initializePlugin` in `add/add.ts` calls

```ts
runPluginInitGenerator(pkgName, workspaceRoot, updatePackageScripts, options.verbose)
```

and `runPluginInitGenerator` (`init/configure-plugins.ts`) builds a fixed command, `g <plugin>:init [--verbose] [--keepExistingVersions] [--updatePackageScripts]`. It has no parameter for extra arguments.

### Expected Behavior

Extra arguments are forwarded to the `init` generator, as they were from 19.0.0 through 20.4.x after #22855 ("fix(core): forward args provided to the nx add command to the invoked init generator"):

```shell
nx add @nx/js --formatter=prettier
# => nx g @nx/js:init --keepExistingVersions ... --formatter=prettier
```

At minimum, `nx add` should fail or warn on arguments it is going to ignore, rather than silently accepting them.

### GitHub Repo

_None needed; reproducible in any workspace._

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `npx create-nx-workspace@latest repro --preset=apps --nxCloud=skip --packageManager=npm --interactive=false`
2. `cd repro`
3. Remove the Prettier setup the template ships with, so the flag has a visible effect: delete `.prettierrc` and the `prettier` devDependency from `package.json`, then commit.
4. `npx nx add @nx/js --formatter=prettier`
   - Result: `Package @nx/js added successfully.` No `.prettierrc` is created and no `prettier` devDependency is added. `git status` shows only `package.json` / `package-lock.json` touched.
5. Control, on a fresh copy from step 3: `npx nx g @nx/js:init --formatter=prettier --keepExistingVersions`
   - Result: `CREATE .prettierrc`, `UPDATE package.json` (adds `"prettier": "~3.6.2"`).

### Nx Report

```
Node           : 24.22.1
OS             : darwin-arm64
Native Target  : aarch64-macos
npm            : 11.19.1
daemon         : Disabled

nx             : 24.0.0
@nx/js         : 24.0.0
@nx/workspace  : 24.0.0
@nx/devkit     : 24.0.0
typescript     : 6.0.3
---------------------------------------
Registered Plugins:
@nx/js/typescript
```

### Failure Logs

```
N/A, no error is printed; the arguments are silently ignored.
```

### Package Manager Version

npm 11.19.1 (the code path is package-manager independent)

### Operating System

- [x] macOS
- [ ] Linux
- [ ] Windows
- [ ] Other (Please specify)

### Additional Information

This looks like an unintended regression from #30029 (`ef08108f7a`, "fix(core): change to use init generator during import", first released in 20.5.0):

- Before that PR, `initializePlugin` parsed `options.__overrides_unparsed__` and passed the result to `installPlugin(..., parsedCommandArgs)`. The PR changed the signature to `(plugin, repoRoot, updatePackageScripts, verbose, pmc)`, which removed the generic options parameter and with it the forwarded args.
- Neither the PR description nor the review mentions removing argument forwarding. In review, the suggestion was to match the older implementation at [`68db3e0` add.ts#L121-L162](https://github.com/nrwl/nx/blob/68db3e032cfe24c66b44a230033fe3032536ba53/packages/nx/src/command-line/add/add.ts#L121-L162), which included `args.push(...options.__overrides_unparsed__)`.
- The plumbing that collects the args (`unknown-options-as-args`, `withOverrides`, `__overrides_unparsed__`) is still in place but unused.

Use case: third-party plugins whose `init` generator needs options (e.g. a program or project name) cannot be installed with a single `nx add <plugin> --option=value`. They have to resort to installing the package and running `nx g <plugin>:init --option=value` separately.

Possible fix: add an `extraArgs: string[] = []` parameter to `runPluginInitGenerator`, append it to the generated command, and pass `options.__overrides_unparsed__` from `initializePlugin`. Happy to open a PR.

items.title: Plan migration of ArtCraft website and Linux repositories from Netlify to Cloudflare
items.body:
## Goal

Move `artcraft-website-next` and its Linux package repository endpoints from Netlify to Cloudflare while keeping existing `https://getartcraft.com` URLs working. Continue to serve downloadable release assets from GitHub Releases so their GitHub download counts remain useful. Do not mirror release binaries to R2 or proxy/cache their bytes through Cloudflare.

This issue covers the public Next.js website and repository endpoints introduced in #204. Inventory the other Netlify sites and services separately; do not assume this change migrates the dashboard, webapp, desktop site, API, media storage, or other infrastructure.

## Current behavior and migration risks

- The Next.js site is deployed through Netlify's Next.js plugin; `netlify.toml` also contains a legacy `/media?media=…` redirect. Verify the equivalent behavior provided in `next.config.ts` works after migration, along with all other redirects, headers, environment variables, image handling, and routes.
- APT (`/apt/...`), RPM (`/rpm/...`), and Pacman (`/arch/...`) metadata is generated by Next.js route handlers. Their package download routes resolve catalogued filenames and return redirects to GitHub Releases. Preserve those allowlists, URLs, redirects and checksums. Test that package-manager downloads actually follow the redirect to GitHub; do not substitute the GitHub asset CDN's temporary signed URL or stream the binary through a Worker.
- Flatpak OCI is different: the current index points at `ghcr.io`, not GitHub Releases. Preserve and test the current Flatpak remote, index and GHCR behavior. GHCR pulls do not become GitHub Releases download counts. Verify that index digests refer to the actual GHCR manifests; do not rely solely on a successful `remote-ls` when an install or pull is required.
- `getRequestBaseUrl` currently explicitly allows Netlify preview origins and loopback, then falls back to production. Replace this with an explicit trusted staging/production origin configuration that works on Cloudflare without trusting arbitrary `Host` or forwarded headers. Audit the `.flatpakref` handler too, which currently constructs an origin from the request URL. Preserve existing production URLs, including trailing paths and HTTPS.
- Index generation currently fetches checksums and package metadata at request time and uses Node APIs (`node:crypto`, `node:zlib`, `Buffer`), in-memory caches and concurrent network requests. Runtime compatibility, cold starts, subrequest limits, CPU/memory usage, and consistency across isolated Workers must be verified. Metadata failures must not silently publish a partial or inconsistent index.
- GitHub release-asset `download_count` is an aggregate, not unique-user analytics; automated checks and retries can affect it. Record a baseline and validate changes empirically, without promising exact attribution. GitHub exposes `download_count` on release assets: https://docs.github.com/en/rest/releases/releases

## Target architecture

1. Deploy the existing Next.js site as a Cloudflare Worker with static assets. Evaluate Cloudflare's recommended vinext path against the actual application; use OpenNext as the first compatibility candidate for the existing Next.js app if it better supports its current features. Choose based on a staging build and feature tests, not a presumed drop-in migration. Cloudflare documents route handlers and Node compatibility for OpenNext: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/framework-guides/web-apps/opennext/
2. Keep production package paths on `getartcraft.com`; retain direct redirects to the original GitHub Release asset URLs. Keep the current GHCR-backed OCI registry for Flatpak unless a separate decision changes it.
3. Produce deterministic repository metadata from a verified release-catalog snapshot at build or release time. Publish matching APT Release/Packages, RPM repomd/primary, Arch databases and OCI metadata as one versioned deployment artifact, with no R2 binary mirror. Preserve old referenced metadata across the maximum cache lifetime, or use immutable/content-addressed paths where client protocols permit; publish new indexes only after referenced files are available. Configure cache TTLs, revalidation and rollback so independently cached index and metadata responses cannot cause checksum mismatches. Verify that the deployment model genuinely preserves old referenced files across version changes; avoid claiming atomic multi-object publication without proving it.
4. Use separate staging and production Workers. Terraform owns stable Cloudflare infrastructure and custom-domain associations; CI/Wrangler owns Worker code, assets and deployments. Do not have Terraform and Wrangler both manage the same Worker or DNS/domain resource. No R2 bucket is required for release artifacts; any adapter-specific cache/storage dependency must be justified separately and must not hold or serve mirrored release binaries.

## Terraform starting point

The example below manages custom domains only. It expects that deployment automation has already created `artcraft-website-staging` and `artcraft-website-production` Workers in the same account. `stage.getartcraft.com` is illustrative; choose an unused hostname. The production resource is deliberately disabled until cutover. Confirm provider/API versions and permissions, review the actual plan, import existing resources if appropriate, and account for any existing DNS records or custom-domain conflicts before applying. Cloudflare manages the DNS record and certificate for a Worker custom domain; do not also create a conflicting Terraform DNS record. See https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/terraform/resources/workers/subresources/domains/ and https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/routing/custom-domains/.

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6.0"

  required_providers {
    cloudflare = {
      source  = "cloudflare/cloudflare"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "cloudflare" {}

variable "cloudflare_account_id" {
  type = string
}

variable "cloudflare_zone_id" {
  type = string
}

variable "staging_hostname" {
  type    = string
  default = "stage.getartcraft.com"
}

variable "production_hostname" {
  type    = string
  default = "getartcraft.com"
}

variable "enable_production_domain" {
  type    = bool
  default = false
}

resource "cloudflare_workers_custom_domain" "staging" {
  account_id       = var.cloudflare_account_id
  zone_id          = var.cloudflare_zone_id
  hostname         = var.staging_hostname
  service          = "artcraft-website-staging"
  enabled          = true
  previews_enabled = false
}

resource "cloudflare_workers_custom_domain" "production" {
  count            = var.enable_production_domain ? 1 : 0
  account_id       = var.cloudflare_account_id
  zone_id          = var.cloudflare_zone_id
  hostname         = var.production_hostname
  service          = "artcraft-website-production"
  enabled          = true
  previews_enabled = false
}

output "staging_url" {
  value = "https://${var.staging_hostname}"
}
```

- Keep Terraform state in the organization's existing secure remote backend with locking and controlled access; do not commit state, tokens or secrets. Use an appropriately scoped Cloudflare API token for Terraform and a separate deployment token for CI.
- Lock and commit the provider version selection. Import existing managed resources as needed and audit the production zone, DNS, certificates, rules, Access/WAF/bot policies and routing before any change. Cloudflare zone ownership and credentials must be confirmed.
- Deploy the Worker before creating its custom-domain association. Keep production disabled in normal staging applies; enable only for the reviewed cutover. If the existing apex configuration cannot be safely replaced this way, define and rehearse the specific DNS/routing transition rather than blindly applying this example.
- Configure build-time public variables (including `NEXT_PUBLIC_GA_MEASUREMENT_ID`) separately from runtime secrets, with production analytics disabled in staging. Use Cloudflare secrets/bindings for sensitive values; do not place them in Terraform code or repository files. Inventory `FLATPAK_OCI_REGISTRY_URL` and every other required environment variable.

## Implementation and validation

1. Inventory current production domain/DNS, Cloudflare account and zone, Netlify settings, environment variables, redirects, headers, cache behavior, required secrets, runtime dependencies, and current monitoring. Confirm what is in scope and where DNS is authoritative. Capture baseline request volume, bandwidth, latency, errors and GitHub asset counts; identify whether Netlify bandwidth is actually attributable to this website or another service.
2. Add pinned Cloudflare adapter/Wrangler dependencies and configuration to the Next.js app, including the appropriate Node compatibility setting, static assets binding and separate staging/production Worker names. Build and deploy a staging version through CI. Do not configure production routes in Wrangler if Terraform owns the domain association. Check supported runtime APIs, package sizes, build size, Workers limits, upstream rate limits, and `Range`/`HEAD` behavior. Document any required paid-plan settings: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/
3. Refactor origin selection and repository metadata generation as described above. Make release/version updates generate and validate the same snapshot across all package indexes. Ensure failure to fetch or validate an upstream checksum fails publication instead of yielding divergent catalogs. Maintain backwards-compatible metadata and cache behavior during rollout and rollback.
4. Parameterize the existing hosted integration checks to run against the staging hostname instead of relying on Netlify-specific preview discovery. Run real APT, DNF, Zypper, Pacman and Flatpak client checks against Cloudflare, including package installation where supported. Validate x86_64 and aarch64 metadata, riscv64 where available, matching hashes and sizes, redirect destinations, unknown-file 404s, and invalid/untrusted host handling.
5. Verify OCI index digests against actual registry manifests, and install or pull an app through the advertised OCI remote for each supported architecture. Check registry authentication, redirects, permissions, tags and manifest/layer digests; distinguish registry problems from website problems.
6. Exercise a release bump with warm caches, concurrent requests, cold Workers and simulated upstream timeout/404. Verify no mixed APT/RPM indexes, stale or missing package links, runtime limit failures or accidental proxying of binary bytes. Compare staging package redirects and production behavior; check representative downloaded files' SHA-256 against their published `SHA256SUMS.txt`.
7. Rehearse production cutover and rollback using staging. Deploy the production Worker without routing traffic, check it via a safe preview/host configuration, then review and apply the production domain change. Verify certificates, redirects, key pages, metadata and real installations immediately. Record the prior DNS/routing configuration, release artifact and cache-purge procedure; keep the Netlify deployment available until rollback is no longer needed. Rollback must restore both routing and matching metadata, not just HTML.
8. Monitor errors, latency, cache behavior, Worker invocations/CPU/subrequests and GitHub download counts after cutover. Account for CI download traffic when comparing counts. Review Cloudflare and GitHub usage costs; remove Netlify resources only after the agreed observation window.

## Acceptance criteria

- Production website and existing Linux repository/Flatpak URLs work on Cloudflare without breaking existing client configuration.
- APT, DNF, Zypper and Pacman package downloads redirect to the expected GitHub Release assets; release binaries are not mirrored to R2 or proxied through Cloudflare. Flatpak OCI remains on GHCR and is validated independently.
- All hosted integration checks pass against Cloudflare staging, including actual installs/pulls and verified checksums/digests. Tests catch untrusted origins and missing or inconsistent metadata.
- Release changes and rollback have been tested under cache overlap without checksum or package-manager failures.
- Terraform changes, deployment ownership, scoped credentials, monitoring, cutover and rollback are documented and reviewed. Production is not switched until staging verification succeeds.


## Illustrative Workers costs

Cloudflare Workers Standard pricing as of 2026-11-01 is $5/month, including 10 million Worker requests and 30 million CPU milliseconds per month. Beyond those allowances, requests cost $0.30 per million and CPU costs $0.02 per million milliseconds. Enterprise contracts and other separately billed services can differ. Source: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/

Assuming every request in the table is billable to Workers, every request executes Worker code, average CPU time is **7 ms per request**, and the account's included allowances are not consumed by other workloads:

| Worker requests per month | Base | Requests | CPU | Estimated total |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 million | $5.00 | $0.00 | $0.00 | $5.00 |
| 10 million | $5.00 | $0.00 | $0.80 | $5.80 |
| 100 million | $5.00 | $27.00 | $13.40 | $45.40 |
| 1 billion | $5.00 | $297.00 | $139.40 | $441.40 |

These are illustrative request-based estimates, not visitor or page-view estimates. The 7 ms figure is Cloudflare's example, not a measurement of this app. Multiple requests can be generated per visit or package update. The paid allowance is shared across account workloads, so incremental costs differ if other Workers consume it.

Cloudflare states that requests served directly as static assets are free and unlimited. With Workers Caching, cached requests remain billable as Worker requests, but cache hits avoid Worker CPU charges; verify the actual deployment and caching behavior. See https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/static-assets/billing-and-limitations/ and the Workers pricing page above.

Package routes should redirect clients to GitHub Releases, so the large release files are transferred from GitHub rather than served by the Worker. Flatpak OCI pulls remain on GHCR. The estimate excludes separately billed services such as image optimization, additional logging, storage or a paid Cloudflare site plan. Before cutover, collect monthly request counts and their breakdown from Netlify, measure staging Worker CPU and cache behavior under representative traffic, and use those observations to build a project-specific estimate. Compare actual costs and GitHub download counts after deployment.


## Suggestion: static metadata and Cloudflare Redirect Rules

Evaluate whether release automation can prebuild the Linux repository metadata and use Cloudflare Redirect Rules for package downloads, reducing Worker requests and CPU. This is an alternative to evaluating every repository request in a Worker; it does not require mirroring binaries. Cloudflare's current Redirect Rules support static and wildcard-based redirects, and Bulk Redirects support large lists of static mappings: https://developers.cloudflare.com/rules/url-forwarding/

**Targeted package download paths:**

- `/apt/pool/.../<filename>.deb` → the exact catalogued GitHub Releases asset URL.
- `/rpm/packages/.../<filename>.rpm` and `/rpm/<arch>/packages/.../<filename>.rpm` → the exact catalogued GitHub Releases asset URL.
- `/arch/<arch>/<filename>.pkg.tar.zst` → the exact catalogued GitHub Releases asset URL. Exclude the Pacman database paths from the package redirect mappings.

Prefer generated exact mappings (or equivalently constrained rules) from the same verified release catalog used to generate the indexes. Preserve the current filename allowlist and 404 behavior for unknown assets; do not create a general open redirect or map arbitrary paths to unverified GitHub URLs. Return a client-visible redirect to the GitHub Release asset, not a URL rewrite or a proxy response, so GitHub continues to serve the binary. Preserve existing supported clients, status codes, request methods and query behavior, and validate rule quotas and changes in Terraform through Scalr.

**Candidate static paths:**

- `/apt/artcraft.sources`, `/apt/artcraft.list`, `/apt/dists/<distribution>/Release`, and `/apt/dists/<distribution>/<component>/<archFolder>/Packages[.gz]`.
- `/rpm/artcraft.repo`, `/rpm/repodata/{repomd.xml,primary.xml.gz}`, and the equivalent `/rpm/<arch>/repodata/...` paths.
- `/arch/artcraft.conf` and `/arch/<arch>/artcraft.db[.tar.gz]`.
- `/artcraft-oci.flatpakrepo` and `/apps/<slug>/<slug>-oci.flatpakref` may be candidates if generated for explicitly configured trusted staging and production origins. Check host selection and existing behavior.

Preserve exact response content, MIME and compression headers, supported paths, 404s, and trusted-origin handling. Generate matching indexes and redirects from one release snapshot, publish safely, and keep previous referenced metadata and GitHub asset redirects available across cache lifetimes and rollback. Verify Cloudflare static-asset and redirect-rule quotas and billing; do not assume deployments are atomic or that old static assets remain available without testing.

Flatpak's OCI index and registry discovery may require query-dependent responses, and OCI artifacts come from GHCR. Assess actual client requests, filtering and manifest digests before deciding whether a static index suffices or a small Worker is necessary; validate with real Flatpak installs/pulls. Other dynamic Next.js website routes may also still require a runtime. Run the existing APT, DNF, Zypper, Pacman and Flatpak integration checks against Cloudflare staging, including release updates with warm caches and rollback.

items.title: Document the deliberate POSIX deviations together

milestone.title: v0.1 — Safe to run on real data
milestone.description:
Answers: can I put data I care about on this and trust what comes back?

Everything here is about the code as it exists today. It closes the gaps where
the filesystem can silently return wrong results, lose buffered writes, or be
bypassed entirely — plus the basics that stop the test suite rotting and make a
running binary identifiable. Nothing here is a new feature; it is the work that
makes the proof of concept honest.

items.body:
Three POSIX behaviours are deliberately absent. They are grouped here because
the decision to revisit them is shared, and because the current state is
*correct but incomplete* rather than broken.

## Hard links

`LINK` returns `NFS3ERR_NOTSUPP`, and FSINFO does not advertise `FSF_LINK`, so
clients know not to try. Supporting them means reference counting inodes
independently of directory entries, which the current namespace can represent
but the commit path does not maintain.

Affects: anything using hard links for atomic replacement or deduplication —
notably `rsync --link-dest`, Maildir, and some package managers.

## Device and socket nodes

`MKNOD` returns `NOTSUPP`. Device nodes have no meaning in an object store, and
inventing one would be worse than refusing. This is very likely permanent, and
the only question is whether to say so more clearly than a status code does.

Affects: extracting an archive containing device nodes, or using the mount as a
root filesystem. Both are out of scope.

## atime

Never updated on read. This is deliberate: the namespace is one document today,
so touching atime would dirty it on every read and force a commit — turning
reads into writes. Linux's `relatime` exists for the same reason.

Affects: anything using atime to find unused files. Rare, and increasingly so,
since `relatime` and `noatime` are near-universal defaults.

## What to do

None of these is urgent. The point of this issue is that the decisions are
currently visible only as scattered code comments, and should be one deliberate
statement in the README under a "what this does not do" heading — so users find
out by reading rather than by a failed command.

After the redesign in `docs/DESIGN.md`, atime becomes affordable (a metadata
block write rather than a whole-namespace rewrite) and hard links become
tractable (the inode file already separates inodes from directory entries), so
this is worth revisiting then.

## Done when

- [ ] All three are documented together in the README
- [ ] A decision is recorded on whether hard links are wanted post-redesign

items.title: Migrate postmarketOS-family ARM64 laptops (apk, LUKS root, ESP at /boot, devicetree) to bootc, reversibly

labels.name: roadmap
labels.description: Approved by a Hive merger/owner for auto-merge on green CI

items.body:
## Goal

Move a running **postmarketOS-family ARM64 laptop** onto a bootc image in place, keeping the user's data, with the old OS bootable until the user commits. The first target machine is a Lenovo ThinkPad X13s running Nura edge (postmarketOS-derived, apk, systemd) going to `ghcr.io/tuna-os/bonito:gnome-x13s` (tuna-os/tunaOS#3788, #3368).

The guarantees of #370 apply unchanged:
- users, home directories, `/etc` changes and application data are carried;
- nothing is destroyed until the user commits;
- the old OS stays bootable as a rollback;
- a report says what moved and what did not.

## Why this machine fails today (main @ 59678261)

`bootc-rebase rebase --dry-run` stops before any change, for these reasons:

| # | Blocker | Where |
|---|---|---|
| B1 | apk is not a package host. Only rpm, dpkg and pacman databases are detected, so the host is `Unknown`. | `source_host.rs` `PACKAGE_DBS`; `package_host.rs` package-manager check |
| B2 | A LUKS root is refused. | `package_host.rs:175` |
| B3 | `/boot` is the ESP. Alongside mode empties `/boot`, which holds the old OS's only kernel, initramfs, DTB and loader entry. The `/boot` snapshot only matches `vmlinuz-*`, `initramfs-*`, `loader/entries/*.conf` and `grub*/grub.cfg`, so it captures none of the pmOS files: `vmlinuz`, `initramfs`, `*.dtb`, `dtbs/`, `loader/`. The early bail ("no package-host kernel was found under /boot") prevents the wipe, so today's failure is a safe one. | `ostree_install.rs` `package_boot_snapshot_paths`; bootc `install.rs` `remove_all_except_loader_dirs` |
| B4 | No "Previous system" entry or `undo` on the package route. | #374, PR #433 (open) |
| B5 | No devicetree or arm64 kernel argument handling. The kargs carry-over keeps only `root=`, `rd.luks.*` and similar. `arm64.nopauth clk_ignore_unused pd_ignore_unused` and the loader's `devicetree` line are dropped. | `filtered_kargs` |
| B6 | No ESP handling on the package route for an ESP mounted at `/boot`. The bind plan exists only for composefs sources (#263). | `ostree_install.rs` ~849 |
| B7 | No aarch64 E2E, and no green package-host cell yet. | `docs/support-matrix.md`, ROADMAP "Unvalidated paths" |

## Measured source layout (read-only probe, 2026-10-23)

- UEFI, **Secure Boot off**, Setup Mode (no PK). No TPM device.
- systemd-boot. ESP = `nvme0n1p1`, 487M vfat, mounted at **`/boot`**, 239M free. Entry `loader/entries/pmos.conf`: `linux vmlinuz`, `initrd initramfs`, `devicetree sc8280xp-lenovo-thinkpad-x13s.dtb`, options `arm64.nopauth clk_ignore_unused pd_ignore_unused pmos_root_uuid=… pmos_boot_uuid=…`.
- Root = `nvme0n1p2`, **LUKS2, argon2id** (GRUB cannot unlock it, #305) → ext4, 468G, 31G used. `crypttab`: `root UUID=… none luks`. No `root=` or `rd.luks.*` on the cmdline; the pmOS initramfs uses `pmos_root_uuid=`.
- Userland: apk, systemd 262, podman, ostree; no bootc. glibc absent (musl), so release binaries for `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` do not run as is.

## Constraint: the ESP is too small for an ESP-resident layout

The target's boot set is about 261M: kernel 17M, initramfs 244M (Fedora's non-hostonly initramfs carries 139M of firmware, including about 100M of NVIDIA GSP files) and the DTB. The ESP has 239M free and 487M in total. So an ESP-resident layout (as #328 does for composefs sources) cannot hold even one deployment, let alone a rollback pair. Either the image ships a small initramfs, or the route needs a `/boot` that is not the ESP.

## Approach

Add a source and a layout to the existing PackageInstall pipeline (#370). This is not a new engine.

1. **apk source.** Detect `/lib/apk/db/installed`. Classify `/etc` with apk's own checksums (`apk audit --system`, or the `Z:` file checksums in the installed db): unmodified packaged files take the target's copy; edits, unpackaged files and machine state carry. Alpine → Fedora is cross-family, so the #256 policy and `--accept-cross-base` apply.
2. **LUKS root, in place.** Reuse the existing container. Derive `rd.luks.uuid=` from `/etc/crypttab` or the dm table, not from the cmdline. Keep `/boot` outside LUKS (argon2id, #305). Refuse when no unencrypted `/boot` or ESP can hold the boot set.
3. **ESP-at-`/boot` layout.** Before bootc runs:
   - snapshot the **whole** ESP (every file, including `*.dtb`, `dtbs/` and `loader/`);
   - give bootc a bind plan in which the ESP is `boot/efi`, as #263 does for composefs;
   - preflight the free space against the target's real boot set size (#440).
4. **Previous system that really boots.** Write a loader entry for the snapshotted kernel, initramfs and DTB, carrying the old `devicetree` line and every old karg. The entry must be for the bootloader that actually starts after the install (systemd-boot stays on this ESP; GRUB if bootupd takes over). Then `undo` restores the ESP snapshot byte for byte and resets `BootOrder` (#374, #433).
5. **Devicetree and arm64 kargs.** Accept the target's own `/usr/lib/modules/$kver/devicetree` (ostree writes a per-deployment `devicetree` line) and `kargs.d`. If the target lacks a DTB while the source boots with one, refuse rather than boot a DT-only laptop with ACPI.
6. **Hardware check on DT platforms.** Compare `/proc/device-tree/compatible` with the DTBs in the target kernel, and the source's loaded firmware (`/lib/firmware/qcom/...`) with the target's. Extends #369, which is PCI/USB oriented.
7. **musl hosts.** Publish an `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` static build (OpenSSL vendored or rustls), or document `gcompat`.

## Plan

| # | Work |
|---|---|
| 1 | apk host detection and `/etc` classifier (B1) |
| 2 | Preflight for a LUKS root with an unencrypted ESP or `/boot`; derive `rd.luks.uuid` (B2) |
| 3 | Whole-ESP snapshot and restore, bind plan, real boot-set space check (B3, B6) |
| 4 | Previous-system entry with `devicetree` and old kargs, and `undo` for the package route (B4, on #433) |
| 5 | Devicetree and arm64 karg policy; refuse when a DT host would lose its DTB (B5) |
| 6 | Hardware check on DT platforms (extends #369) |
| 7 | `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` release artifact |
| 8 | E2E: arm64 VM cell with a pmOS-like layout (LUKS2 argon2id ext4 root, ESP at `/boot`, systemd-boot with a `devicetree` entry) on `ubuntu-24.04-arm`: migrate, reboot into the target, `undo`, reboot into the source (B7) |
| 9 | Real-hardware qualification on an X13s, recorded in the support matrix |

TunaOS side (tuna-os/tunaOS#3368): a hostonly-sized or firmware-trimmed initramfs for `bonito:gnome-x13s`, so the boot set fits a small ESP. The image already ships the X13s DTB as `devicetree`, `kargs.d` and the early-boot modules (#3788).

## Principles

- **Nothing on the ESP is changed before a complete snapshot exists on a different filesystem.** `undo` must restore the old boot chain byte for byte.
- **A gap in a check is not a pass.** If the boot set does not fit, or the target has no DTB for a DT host, refuse before any change.
- **No distribution names in the logic** (#258). Classify by package database (apk), by loader entries and by what a path is.
- **One engine.** apk and the ESP-at-`/boot` layout are a source and a layout for the existing PackageInstall pipeline.

## Decisions (maintainer, 2026-10-24)

1. **Bootloader: systemd-boot.** The source already boots through systemd-boot with a `devicetree` line.
2. **Shared ESP, pmOS-compatible layout.** TunaOS and pmOS share the ESP, and systemd-boot lists both. bootc's composefs Type 1 layout does not collide with pmOS files: its kernels go in `EFI/Linux/bootc_<id>/{vmlinuz,initrd}` (bootc `bootc_composefs/boot.rs:920-934, 715-738`) and its entries are `loader/entries/bootc_*.conf`, while pmOS keeps `vmlinuz`, `initramfs`, `*.dtb`, `dtbs/` and `loader/entries/pmos.conf` at the ESP root.
3. **Backend: composefs.** The first image need not be bonito (ostree/GRUB). The arm64 candidate is `marlin`, which already ships systemd-boot (`50-marlin.toml` `bootloader = "systemd"`), a sealed composefs root and ext4. Bluefin Utah is amd64-only (single-arch manifest), so it cannot be the X13s's first image.

## bootc upstream gaps for the shared-ESP layout (bootc-dev/bootc @ 69057a8)

| # | Gap | Where | Needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| U1 | `to-existing-root` empties all of `/boot` on a non-ostree source, then removes the ESP's `EFI/` and `loader/`. When `/boot` is the ESP, this deletes pmOS's kernel, initramfs, DTBs, `pmos.conf` and its systemd-boot. | `install.rs:2563-2611` (`remove_all_except_loader_dirs`, `clean_esp_bootloader_dirs`); bootc's own TODO at :2600 (#2243) | Keep foreign ESP content and non-bootc `loader/entries` |
| U2 | Every upgrade replaces `loader/entries` with a staged directory that holds only bootc's two entries, so `pmos.conf` disappears at the first `bootc upgrade`. | `bootc_composefs/rollback.rs:63-77` (`rename_exchange_bls_entries`); staged dir `boot.rs:1047-1059` | Copy non-bootc entries into `entries.staged` before the exchange |
| U3 | The composefs Type 1 writer emits no `devicetree` key and copies no DTB. | `boot.rs:966-981` (BLS fields), `:707-748` (files written) | Copy `/usr/lib/modules/$kver/devicetree` into `EFI/Linux/bootc_<id>/` and add `devicetree`; or UKIs with `.dtbauto` (systemd already ships X13s hwids) |
| U4 | `loader/loader.conf` default and timeout are owned by bootc. | `boot.rs` `SYSTEMD_LOADER_CONF_PATH` | Leave `timeout` alone, or document the takeover |

Until U1 is fixed, bootc-migrate must snapshot the whole ESP and restore pmOS's files and entry after `bootc install`. Until U2 is fixed, it must restore them after each upgrade (or ship a hook). Neither is acceptable as the long-term answer, so U1 and U2 belong upstream.

## Additional source and image items found

- **ext4 fs-verity:** a sealed composefs root needs fs-verity, but pmOS's ext4 may lack the `verity` feature. The preflight must check it, and enable it where safe (`tune2fs -O verity`) or refuse.
- **ESP space:** pmOS uses 247M of 487M. One TunaOS boot set is about 208M (marlin: initramfs 160M + kernel 48M) or 261M (bonito). A rollback pair with a different kernel does not fit, so the X13s image needs a trimmed initramfs (tuna-os/tunaOS#3368). bootc already shares identical kernel/initrd pairs between deployments (`boot.rs:983-1028`).
- **marlin arm64** lacks the X13s DTB and qcom firmware. The TunaOS work is a `marlin:gnome-x13s` profile: DTB, `linux-firmware-qcom`, `kargs.d`, early-boot modules and a trimmed initramfs.

Related: #370 (package hosts), #374 / PR #433 (previous system and undo), #305 / #328 (LUKS and ESP-resident entries), #263 (ESP bind plan), #369 (hardware check), #440 (free space), #256 / #258 (cross-family policy).

items.title: Linux native packages (rpm, deb) not adhering to best practice and misleading/unused packaging templates
items.body:
I've been messing around with rpm packaging recently and I noticed some weird stuff that I didn't expect. On a deeper dive I noticed this is a bit wider in scope than I assumed and also affects our .deb package as well as our .desktop file (which can be found in this issue: https://github.com/pulsar-edit/pulsar/issues/1580

## RPM 
Grabbed our latest released rpm and queried it:

```sh
> rpm -qp --info Linux.pulsar-1.132.1.x86_64.rpm
Name        : pulsar
Version     : 1.132.1
Release     : 1
Architecture: x86_64
Install Date: (not installed)
Group       : default
Size        : 798751807
License     : MIT
Signature   : (none)
Source RPM  : pulsar-1.132.1-1.src.rpm
Build Date  : Wed 20 May 2026 20:43:29 BST
Build Host  : 96c2619dee49
Relocations : /
Packager    : Pulsar-Edit <admin@pulsar-edit.dev>
Vendor      : Pulsar-Edit <admin@pulsar-edit.dev>
URL         : https://github.com/pulsar-edit/pulsar#readme
Summary     : A community-led hyper-hackable text editor
Description :
A Community-led Hyper-Hackable Text Editor
```

Which struck me as a little odd as not much of this ties into our own, maintained, [rpm spec template](https://github.com/pulsar-edit/pulsar/blob/91421974a1a75b3b5e5acd01835e0f401dba1135/resources/linux/redhat/pulsar.spec.in). The URL is different for a start.

Annoyingly `fpm` as used by `electron-builder` doesn't really make a proper .spec file but we can at least see the installed files with `rpm -qp --list Linux.pulsar-1.132.1.x86_64.rpm` which shows that we literally install everything to `/opt/Pulsar` with the exception of the icon files in `/usr/share` (files cut for brevity):
```sh
> rpm -qp --list Linux.pulsar-1.132.1.x86_64.rpm
/opt/Pulsar/chrome-sandbox
/opt/Pulsar/chrome_100_percent.pak
/opt/Pulsar/chrome_200_percent.pak
...
/opt/Pulsar/resources/pulsar.sh
/usr/share/applications/pulsar.desktop
/usr/share/icons/hicolor/128x128/apps/pulsar.png
...
```

But in our existing rpm spec template, `/opt` is not specified at all, and whilst not the greatest place to put software it is technically ok for a manually distributed .rpm like ours:

https://github.com/pulsar-edit/pulsar/blob/91421974a1a75b3b5e5acd01835e0f401dba1135/resources/linux/redhat/pulsar.spec.in#L55-L62

If we compare this to the 1.60.0 release of Atom we actually find that not only the package info but also the installed files actually do conform to the spec template. The majority of the application installs to `/usr/share` whilst the the `pulsar.sh` goes into `/usr/bin` without a postinstall script being needed as we currently do.

```
cp -r "<%= appName %>"/* "%{buildroot}/<%= installDir %>/share/<%= appFileName %>/"
cp pulsar.sh "%{buildroot}/<%= installDir %>/bin/<%= appFileName %>"
```

## DEB

So if I crack open a .deb we produce and have a look at its `control` file:
```
Package: pulsar
Version: 1.132.1
License: MIT
Vendor: Pulsar-Edit <admin@pulsar-edit.dev>
Architecture: amd64
Maintainer: Pulsar-Edit <admin@pulsar-edit.dev>
Installed-Size: 783597
Depends: libgtk-3-0, libnotify4, libnss3, libxss1, libxtst6, xdg-utils, libatspi2.0-0, libuuid1, libsecret-1-0
Recommends: libappindicator3-1
Section: default
Priority: optional
Homepage: https://github.com/pulsar-edit/pulsar#readme
Description: A community-led hyper-hackable text editor
  A Community-led Hyper-Hackable Text Editor
```

It too doesn't actually match our control template:

https://github.com/pulsar-edit/pulsar/blob/91421974a1a75b3b5e5acd01835e0f401dba1135/resources/linux/debian/control.in#L1-L12

So this too hasn't actually been generated from the template. Now with the deb package I need to plead ignorance as I don't actually know where it is *meant* to be installed by the code alone. I'm on a journey plunging the depths of rpm right now so I've not got the bandwidth (yet) to understand how the deb actually gets packaged BUT if we crack the Atom 1.60.0 deb file open we do indeed see that it too is meant to go into `/usr` and not `/opt`:

```
.
└── usr
    ├── bin
    │   ├── apm -> ../share/atom/resources/app/apm/node_modules/.bin/apm
    │   └── atom
    └── share
        ├── applications
        ├── atom
        ├── doc
        ├── pixmaps
        └── polkit-1
```

## So what is going on?

Honestly I can't be certain but when we moved from whatever Atom was doing to build their packages to our `electron-builder` workflow, I think we didn't actually match up our new format to the old ones. Not using the control and spec templates isn't a problem by itself but we never actually took any of that information that they provide and implemented them into our `electron-builder` workflow.

This means that, whilst we do specify *some* options, the rest reverts back to `electron-builder` defaults - reading from the `package.json` and throwing everything into `/opt`.

There is further evidence for this in that we also have an issue with our `.desktop` file which follows this exact same pattern - we don't use the template and instead just default a whole bunch of stuff.

## What problems does this cause?

Evidently not many. This is less about trying to fix an overtly "broken" issue and more about 1) documenting that this seems to have happened at all and 2) updating our build process so that some of the more important information isn't left out. 

The other part is that it does hold us to better practices. For example what we do with rpm, installing to `/opt` and moving the `pulsar.sh` via a scriptlet isn't really a good thing to do and can lead to untracked files. This is particularly important if we wish to actually distribute via actual package repositories.

I see this as similar to the desire to adhere to the XDG Base Directory Specification. We *should* be adhering to good practice for the packages we provide if we are going to provide them.

## What should we do?

So I think there are some easy wins and some harder ones here:

1. We should update our `electron-builder` packaging workflow to actually specify certain fields that are used in the rpm spec and Debian `control`. These are mostly entirely informational or add small bits of additional functionality like more accurate package install requirements
2. Consider migrating from the existing `/opt` install location to the originally intended locations from Atom in `/usr`. This is better packaging practice in general, particularly if provided by an actual package manager rather than just installing the package manually.

The obvious problem with 2. is that it will affect existing user installs. We would need to account for making sure that it actually first removes the old install before installing over it. Or at the very least refuse to install unless the old package is manually uninstalled first. I also don't know if there are any other side effects from this regarding functionality that relies on it being placed in `/opt`. It would also likely affect community package maintainers who would need to adjust how their packages are constructed.

### Pulsar version

1.132.1

### Which OS does this happen on?

🐧 Red Hat based (Fedora, Alma, RockyLinux, CentOS Stream, etc.)

### OS details

Fedora 43

### Which CPU architecture are you running this on?

x86_64/AMD64

### What steps are needed to reproduce this?

N/A

### Additional Information:

_No response_

### Closeout review — 2026-10-26

**Status: Partial implementation or follow-up acceptance remains.**

Work needed before closure:

- [ ] Register these as capability-scoped requirements in the shared provisioning plan, with one resolver/identity/verification contract used by consumer, doctor and installer. A selected workflow must offer/execute its authorized setup plan; do not silently say optional and skip a requested output. Unselected features must not trigger mass installation.
- [ ] Semgrep: pinned supported package in a managed Python tool environment with compatible Python and supported platform, explicit local rule mode and no implicit login/cloud upload. ast-grep: install the actual pinned CLI through upstream npm/binary distribution; prefer the unambiguous ast-grep command and positively identify it before accepting sg. Comby: official supported distribution with native-platform classification; WSL/container setup is a separate explicit system choice, never silently enable it.
- [ ] Graphviz: official archive where supported (Windows packages include ZIP plus SHA256), otherwise a concrete supported package-manager/system step. Verify dot -V, shared libraries/plugins/fonts required for the selected renderer and a tiny in-memory DOT-to-SVG operation; presence alone is insufficient. Preserve DOT-only as an explicit user choice, not a disguised successful SVG request.
- [ ] TUI: detect/reuse a compatible selected Rust/Cargo toolchain, or provision in owned homes through the Rust recipe; separately identify missing native linker/SDK. Release tooling: pin cargo-cyclonedx, verify the cargo subcommand identity/schema and npm SBOM capability only for the release workflow. LFS/rg: detect existing tools and provision only when selected/needed, retaining the documented safe fallback for optional acceleration.
- [ ] Pass the related existing checks and the complete original/follow-up acceptance on the resulting candidate; preserve positive and negative controls.

Current source owners: [`src/experimental/structural/binaries.js`](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/accf98f64a560a5df9b1bdb175f7ca22331672af/src/experimental/structural/binaries.js), [`tools/reports/report-code-map.js`](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/accf98f64a560a5df9b1bdb175f7ca22331672af/tools/reports/report-code-map.js), [`tools/tui/build-support.js`](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/accf98f64a560a5df9b1bdb175f7ca22331672af/tools/tui/build-support.js).

Related checks (starting points; not execution evidence): `tooling/install/structural-engine-identity`, `tooling/docs/authored-recipes-contract`, `tooling/install/provisioning-runtime-identity`, `tooling/install/tool-install-receipt-drift`.

Keep this issue open until its original requirements and follow-up acceptance are demonstrated on the resulting candidate.

[Issue assessment and evidence](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/f8532f1d2e54597feecf017e3a60d9ae3258762c/docs/archived/github-issue-closeout-2026-10-26.json#L815) · [Audit overview](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/f8532f1d2e54597feecf017e3a60d9ae3258762c/docs/archived/github-issue-closeout-2026-10-26.md).
<!-- poc-issue-closeout:end -->

---

## Source-backed missing catalog coverage
The 24-entry language-tool registry omits several executables consumed by shipped workflows:
- [Structural search](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/src/experimental/structural/binaries.js): Semgrep, ast-grep CLI and Comby. Detection is a separate PATH-only resolver; POSIX accepts any successful version/help response, and `sg` is tried before `ast-grep`. The installed `@ast-grep/napi` library is not proof the external CLI exists.
- [Graph rendering](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/reports/report-code-map.js): Graphviz `dot` for SVG, distinct from DOT-only output.
- [TUI source build](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/tui/build-support.js): Cargo/Rust plus host linker/build prerequisites, although artifact staging/build already exists. Do not reopen completed #316.
- [Release trust material](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/release/generate-trust-materials.js): `cargo cyclonedx` and npm's SBOM command capabilities.
- [Dictionary discovery](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/dicts/generate-repo-dict.js): `rg` is an accelerator with an actual fallback, not an unconditional core prerequisite.
- [Benchmark source preparation](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/bench/language/repos.js): Git LFS only for selected repositories that need LFS; ordinary Git is already a core bootstrap prerequisite.

## Required behavior
- [ ] Register these as capability-scoped requirements in the shared provisioning plan, with one resolver/identity/verification contract used by consumer, doctor and installer. A selected workflow must offer/execute its authorized setup plan; do not silently say optional and skip a requested output. Unselected features must not trigger mass installation.
- [ ] Semgrep: pinned supported package in a managed Python tool environment with compatible Python and supported platform, explicit local rule mode and no implicit login/cloud upload. ast-grep: install the actual pinned CLI through upstream npm/binary distribution; prefer the unambiguous `ast-grep` command and positively identify it before accepting `sg`. Comby: official supported distribution with native-platform classification; WSL/container setup is a separate explicit system choice, never silently enable it.
- [ ] Graphviz: official archive where supported (Windows packages include ZIP plus SHA256), otherwise a concrete supported package-manager/system step. Verify `dot -V`, shared libraries/plugins/fonts required for the selected renderer and a tiny in-memory DOT-to-SVG operation; presence alone is insufficient. Preserve DOT-only as an explicit user choice, not a disguised successful SVG request.
- [ ] TUI: detect/reuse a compatible selected Rust/Cargo toolchain, or provision in owned homes through the Rust recipe; separately identify missing native linker/SDK. Release tooling: pin cargo-cyclonedx, verify the cargo subcommand identity/schema and npm SBOM capability only for the release workflow. LFS/rg: detect existing tools and provision only when selected/needed, retaining the documented safe fallback for optional acceleration.
- [ ] Record platform/architecture, exact executable, dependencies, installation scope and receipts; route caches via #1268. Use app-owned destinations by default. Any system package action clearly names packages, manager, privilege/terms and resumable next step.
- [ ] Add recipes for the actually supported execution forms of [ctags ingest](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/ingest/ctags.js), [GTAGS ingest](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/ingest/gtags.js) and [SCIP ingest](https://github.com/doublemover/PairOfCleats/blob/8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda/tools/ingest/scip.js): Universal Ctags with required JSON/output-field capabilities, GNU Global's scoped query command and the selected SCIP CLI command. Distinguish these from reading file/stdin reports, which must require no producer installation. LSIF file ingest likewise needs no external producer. For explicit execution, provision a compatible official/reputable release and pass the verified exact command; do not run an arbitrary same-named system ctags/global. Report absence of an upstream platform recipe concretely rather than claiming native support. Project indexing/query execution remains separately scoped.

## Verified upstream basis
[ast-grep quick start](https://ast-grep.github.io/guide/quick-start.html) documents its CLI package and the Linux `sg` name collision. [Semgrep quick start](https://docs.semgrep.dev/getting-started/quickstart) gives its Python requirement; current supported-platform documentation must determine the chosen package. [Comby installation](https://comby.dev/docs/get-started) documents macOS, Ubuntu and Windows-via-WSL routes, not native-Windows parity. [Graphviz downloads](https://graphviz.org/download/) distinguishes platform packages and portable Windows archives. [Rustup](https://rust-lang.github.io/rustup/installation/index.html) supports scoped toolchain homes. Pin and verify currently supported assets at implementation time; these sources are not proof of execution.

## Acceptance
End-to-end tiny selected workflows: local Semgrep/ast-grep/Comby matches; Graphviz SVG; TUI build/install/launch; release SBOM schema; LFS prerequisite diagnosis. Test unrelated `sg`, stale PATH/changed executable, missing shared library, absent Python/Cargo, unsupported platform, denied system action, offline install and already-installed no-download reuse. Consumer must resolve the tool just installed without global PATH edits. Report pass/fail/unrun by platform; missing capability is not a successful empty result.

Dedup: reviewed structural/Graphviz/install/toolchain issues, #1271 docs, #1262 onboarding, #316 completed build/staging, #631 language-tool qualification and #681 unused dependency cleanup. None owns feature-scoped provisioning of these operational executables.

## Scope and qualification
Source-only audit of PR #572 at `8685a0decb70fde42f32896f52825009c5970dda` on 2026-10-22, with relevant current files fetched through GitHub and existing issue bodies reviewed. No implementation, installation on a user machine, or real cross-platform qualification was performed. Implement against the current supported Node/bootstrap contract and use bounded focused fixtures; record real Windows/macOS/Linux and architecture coverage separately. This is implementation work, not an index/umbrella ticket. Use a modern canonical cutover, not permanent legacy aliases, parallel registries or silent legacy-product fallbacks.

items.body:
### Steps to reproduce

An unmodified `flutter create` app kills the Android emulator it runs on, about a
second after Impeller selects the GLES backend. Not the app process — the host
`qemu-system-x86_64-headless` process, on an x86_64 Linux emulator running
`-gpu swangle_indirect`. Disabling Impeller avoids it; 3.41.9 does not show it.

## Steps to reproduce

1. On an **x86_64 Linux** host, start an Android emulator headless with the
   software renderer:
   ```console
   emulator -avd <name> -no-window -no-audio -no-boot-anim -gpu swangle_indirect
   ```
2. Create and build a stock app, unmodified:
   ```console
   flutter create --org com.example --project-name impellerrepro --platforms android repro_app
   cd repro_app && flutter build apk --release
   ```
3. Install and launch it:
   ```console
   adb -s emulator-5554 install -r build/app/outputs/flutter-apk/app-release.apk
   adb -s emulator-5554 shell monkey -p com.example.impellerrepro -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1
   ```
4. Watch the host, not the guest:
   ```console
   while :; do adb devices; ps -Ao pid,etime,command | grep qemu-system; sleep 1; done
   ```

### Expected results

The counter app renders. If Impeller cannot drive the host GL stack, the engine
falls back or the app crashes — either way the emulator keeps running.

### Actual results

The emulator disappears about **3 seconds** after launch, roughly **1 second**
after the engine selects the GLES backend. It vanishes from `adb devices`
entirely (`device 'emulator-5554' not found`, never `offline`), and its host
process is gone.

```
15:54:43.411  W/Monkey   args: [-p, com.example.impellerrepro, -c, android.intent.category.LAUNCHER, 1]
15:54:43.609  I/flutter  [IMPORTANT:flutter/shell/platform/android/android_context_gl_impeller.cc(104)]
                         Using the Impeller rendering backend (OpenGLES).
15:54:44.681  I/Choreographer  Skipped 66 frames!
              <logcat ends here — no exception, no ANR, no tombstone>
```

Seven emulators were running on the host; the app was launched on one of them.
Exactly that one died:

```
qemu pids before:  100023 100181 100182  99808  99809 99810 99811
qemu pids after :  100023 100181 100182         99809 99810 99811
```

The six idle siblings were untouched, which rules out host pressure or a
supervisor restarting everything. The host had 32 cores, 126 GB RAM and unused
swap at the time.

### Scope

- Setting `io.flutter.embedding.android.EnableImpeller` to `false` in the

## Current status — 29 October 2026

Mitigation #185 is merged after exact-head CI passed on both architectures. Release v0.6.3 includes the validated change. The issue remains open for residual OS reports rather than claiming a vulnerability-free image.

### Measured reduction

Snyk Container rescans of the published `ghcr.io/luen/crag-stats:0.6.3` images on both amd64 and arm64 confirm:
- OS dependencies: 91 → 14.
- Unique OS advisory IDs: 96 → 25.
- Severity: **1 critical / 5 high / 2 medium / 88 low → 0 critical / 1 high / 0 medium / 24 low**.
- Packaged application project: 8 detected dependencies, no vulnerable paths.
- No fixedIn version is listed for the remaining OS reports. No ignores added.

The released image uses supported distroless Debian 13 C++ runtime libraries with the Node 24 binary copied from the existing build stage, removing unused mount/admin utilities and shells. Existing volume ownership is retained. It has no shell or package manager.

### Source-based triage

- Former critical CVE-2023-45853 concerns MiniZip. Debian's Bookworm notes explain that its zlib binaries do not build that vulnerable component: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/CVE-2023-45853
- Remaining raw high SNYK-DEBIAN13-ZLIB-19520500 / CVE-2026-85091 is reported against zlib 1:1.3.dfsg+really1.3.1-1+b1. Our source-based assessment is not affected: gz_vacate was introduced with non-blocking writes in upstream 1.3.1.2 and is absent from the installed Debian 1.3.1 source. The Debian tracker still labels it vulnerable; retain the raw finding while this discrepancy is clarified.
  - Packaged source: https://sources.debian.org/src/zlib/1:1.3.dfsg%2Breally1.3.1-1/gzwrite.c/
  - Introducing commit: https://github.com/madler/zlib/commit/81cc0bebedd935daeb81b0b6e475d8786b51af3d

### Validation

Both architecture candidates built and passed SQLite, migrations, sample CSV import, logbook HTTP, real impers native loading, compressed loopback requests and HTTPS certificate checks without contacting theCrag. A later local Docker restart lost arm64 emulation even for the official Node image; clean CI arm64 smoke tests subsequently passed, including on the final release commit. v0.6.3 and latest share manifest digest `sha256:938c58ea9dfcf20c513c29bbe85e59693897adae4156fb84359eb6e4cbe550f0`. Both published scans found 14 OS dependencies / 25 IDs (0 critical, 1 high, 24 low), plus 8 application dependencies with no vulnerable paths. # BN5 — Bun-first CLI, development loop and native CI

**Standalone agent brief — no previous conversation required.** Bun Native is a complete rewrite of the disposable Bunly/CEF project in `0xPlayerOne/bun-native`. Build a TypeScript-first, JavaScript-compatible desktop framework around **Bun**, **browserless native UI** (Rust GPUI is the initial renderer), **machine-code Bun AOT for production**, and first-party **SolidJS + React** adapters. App authors must not need Rust or a native rebuild after ordinary TS/JS edits. The old CEF/WebView code is not a fallback. An agent can change the native implementation engine with technical evidence and an ADR.

**Autonomy:** the owner authorizes agents to change/delete experimental repository code, architecture, dependencies, CI, issues, PRs and release tooling without routine human approvals. Open draft PRs with initial commits, push continuously, prepare review and enable auto-merge when GitHub checks permit. If a dependency fails, reproduce/repair or track it and advance independent tasks. No Adea production or personal Mac data changes are authorized. Test on GitHub-hosted Linux/Windows/macOS first; use the connected Mac via Remote Desktop Commander when actual GUI input is needed. Keep Docker on the Mac limited and temporary. Do not claim tests that were skipped or impossible.


**Cold-start rule:** If assigned this milestone with zero prior context, read this epic and its linked task issues, inspect the real repository/PR/CI state and verify prerequisite artifacts rather than assuming earlier milestones are complete. If a required dependency is missing, implement or repair the earliest missing prerequisite autonomously, then return to this epic. Use actual available tools and version-pinned evidence; do not wait for the owner or claim a missing prerequisite passed.
## Entry state and goal

BN0 (#217) must retire the old CEF workflow triggers and start honest minimal native checks in #251; this stage expands them into the full multi-platform framework developer experience. BN1 defines the public host ABI; BN2/BN3 expose Solid and React adapters. A developer should be able to create, run, edit, test and package a Bun Native app **without knowing Rust**.

## Work items

- [ ] **#240 — Bun toolchain integration:** actual built-in Bun typecheck/format/test, package-manager scripts, production `bun compile` AOT, deterministic errors and a separate development run mode. Avoid confusing package scripts named `check`/`fmt` with built-ins.
- [ ] **#242 — CLI and starter templates:** discoverable create/dev/build/test/doctor commands (final CLI naming decided by implementer), TS-default and JS-compatible examples for Solid/React, native artifact resolution and clean-install diagnostics.
- [ ] **#243 — Fast edit loop:** watch/reload TS/TSX changes without rerunning Cargo or replacing the native renderer unnecessarily. Define state-retention/remount/full-restart boundaries, callback disposal and benchmark edit-to-usable time.
- [ ] **#256 — Full GitHub Actions native CI:** expand BN0 bootstrap checks into Bun/Rust unit, ABI integration, compiler AOT vs JIT canary, actual native window smoke, macOS/Windows/Linux hosted runner packaging and artifacts. Remove obsolete M1–M6 workflows/required contexts through #251 and adjust new check requirements without removing meaningful validation.

- [ ] **#259 — Automated code-health and performance gates:** enforce dependency/unused-code checks and version-pinned regression suites; keep PR feedback fast and deeper soak in scheduled/release CI.

## Done means

- Fresh TS and JS Solid/React projects can be generated, installed, run and compiled from documented commands on supported platforms; missing native artifacts produce actionable errors.
- Ordinary TS/JS edits update the native app without invoking Rust/Cargo; repeated reloads clean listeners/resources and have measured latency and stability.
- Production build uses **real Bun AOT**, not a JIT-packaged executable renamed as native; compiler/library incompatibilities are explicit.
- Native host versions and prebuilt binaries are pinned/compatible with consumer package versions; failure/restart behavior is documented.
- Hosted CI provides independent tests and artifacts for supported targets. A test that only compiles or simulates UI cannot count as an interactive GPU-window pass. Use the connected Mac for real GUI checks when hosted runners fall short.
- Invalid type/format/test fixtures fail CI intentionally; old Bunly checks no longer determine Bun Native success.

## Automated quality checkpoint (no human sign-off)

Follow [the engineering-quality standard](https://github.com/0xPlayerOne/bun-native/blob/60694ce7cbf1635d9164c9d024736b5423198b55/docs/engineering-quality.md). Run clean-template create/dev/build/test flows, 100+ UI reloads with no unexplained resource growth, dev edit-to-usable latency, compiler AOT slow-path diagnostics, and changed-package dead-code/boundary scans. Measure CI wall time/cache behavior; preserve a fast PR lane and independent full native/GPU matrix. No stale CEF scripts.

Record exact tests, versions, platform, metrics, code cleanup and any remaining measurable regression in this epic/linked PRs. Investigate and fix significant unexplained regressions or document a justified measured tradeoff; keep other unblocked work moving.

## Handoff

CLI/artifact rules feed **BN6 #246** distribution. Stable reload, native CI and templates feed **BN7** adoption/docs. Do not wait for a human to validate a local GUI—automate hosted or Desktop Commander checks and mark unavailable coverage honestly. Roadmap: #1.

items.title: [P2] Commit SDK activation through one generation pointer
items.body:
**Pre-publication head recheck (2026-10-29):** The bounded delta from `125785329d97b590447379a45768e9ec04ba29d6` to `45e37d7d1decc9e1cc7940c7171a710e17fbf1d0` contains two commits and 16 changed paths. **This finding remains applicable.** The exact two-commit comparison does not change any repository blob cited by this finding. Original pinned evidence and prior rechecks below are retained. This is static source/hash review, not a build, test execution or runtime reproduction.

**Freshness recheck (2026-10-29):** PR #8278 advanced to `125785329d97b590447379a45768e9ec04ba29d6`. A bounded [old-to-new comparison](https://github.com/doublemover/Slopjective-C/compare/0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482...125785329d97b590447379a45768e9ec04ba29d6) confirms the implementation files underlying this finding are unchanged. The manifest changed only patch digests; its upstream LLVM pin is unchanged, and the changed patch packets do not alter lit or dependency-file callbacks. The finding remains applicable; original audited source anchors are preserved. This was a static delta check, not an executed reproduction.

## Finding and scope

The SDK installer publishes the selected generation twice: first through `current`, then through a separately replaced `activate.sh` containing the concrete SDK path. A failure or interruption between those writes leaves the two public entrypoints selecting different SDK generations. This is a recoverability/coherence defect, **not** a claim that the installer falsely returns PASS or that archive verification is bypassed.

Reviewed head: `0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482`, PR #8278. Static-only, high confidence in the split publication path; no fault injection, installation, builds or tests executed.

## Invariant and source proof

After a completed activation, newly resolving `root/current` and newly sourcing `root/activate.sh` should select the same verified SDK. A failed update should not leave a persistent disagreement between those two current-selection interfaces.

- [`install_sdk.activate():34–43`](https://github.com/doublemover/Slopjective-C/blob/0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482/scripts/objc3c_toolchain/install_sdk.py#L34-L43) creates a temporary symlink and immediately `os.replace`s it over `root/current`.
- [`activate():44–64`](https://github.com/doublemover/Slopjective-C/blob/0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482/scripts/objc3c_toolchain/install_sdk.py#L44-L64) subsequently constructs shell text whose `OBJC3C_SDK_ROOT` is the absolute concrete `prefix`, writes/chmods a pending file, and separately replaces `root/activate.sh`. Its `finally` removes the pending file; it does not restore `current`.
- [`install():97–110`](https://github.com/doublemover/Slopjective-C/blob/0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482/scripts/objc3c_toolchain/install_sdk.py#L97-L110) verifies/stores the new generation before calling `activate`. On error, the caller reports failure; there is no atomic combined publication or repair in that error path.
- This is not an unused pointer: [`linux_sdk.py:145–153`](https://github.com/doublemover/Slopjective-C/blob/0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482/scripts/objc3c_toolchain/linux_sdk.py#L145-L153) discovers the active foundation through `install_root/current`. The documented user route sources `activate.sh`, which instead selects the embedded concrete prefix.
- [`test_toolchain_install.py`](https://github.com/doublemover/Slopjective-C/blob/0cb07601ca1c745b1a8158b76959b56ffd0ee482/tests/tooling/test_toolchain_install.py) checks preservation on bad archive/tampered-prefix admission and ordinary reuse/relocation; it does not inject failures between these two publication operations. Keep those existing tests.

## Minimal counterexample / proposed fault-injection test

Start from a successful generation A: `current -> sdks/A`, `activate.sh` exports `.../sdks/A`. Install a verified generation B. Let creation/replacement of `.current-<pid>` succeed, then make the following `.activate-<pid>` write fail with `ENOSPC`, or terminate the process at that boundary.

Final persistent state under the current code:

```
root/current       -> sdks/B
root/activate.sh   -> shell text exporting root/sdks/A
```

A newly opened shell sourcing the documented activation file uses A, whereas code using the advertised current symlink discovers B. On a first installation the corresponding boundary can leave `current` present with no activation file. Both generation payloads remain intact; the bug is their inconsistent selection. The current README's narrow statement that `current` switches atomically is technically true, so do not misquote it as an explicit guarantee of a two-file transaction.

Re-running installation can repair the state, and pending-qualified-archive resumption already preserves a route to do so. That useful recovery does not make the failed operation leave coherent activation before the retry. No data-loss or malicious-code claim is needed.

## Repair design

Use **one authoritative atomic pointer** for generation selection. For example, a stable root activation script can resolve `root/current` once at source time and export the resulting concrete verified prefix; then only changing `current` publishes an update. Alternatively, publish versioned activation metadata selected by the same pointer. Preserve bootstrap/product separation, shell quoting, root-install permissions and existing-shell pinning semantics.

Prepare and validate all other required state before committing that pointer. Merely swapping the order of the current two writes reverses the disagreement window; try/except rollback alone does not handle process termination. On failure before commit, A remains selected; after commit, both interfaces resolve B. Keep A installed, and make explicit rollback/reinstall select an already verified generation through the same mechanism.

Do not repoint already-running shells unexpectedly. The target property is coherence for **new reads/sourcing** at a given generation, not retroactively replacing every process environment. Ordinary linearizable reads across a concurrent update may observe A or B; they must not remain split after the updater has failed/stopped.

## Acceptance

1. Inject failure at every pre-commit file creation/write/chmod/rename and at post-commit cleanup. A fresh `current` read and freshly sourced activation must identify one coherent generation.
2. Include termination between filesystem operations, not only catchable Python exceptions; retry remains safe and idempotent.
3. Test first install, A→B update, B→A rollback/reinstall, same-generation reuse and relocated root.
4. Exercise spaces/quotes in the root, restrictive umask and unprivileged consumers of root-owned installations.
5. Existing archive-checksum, cached-verifier admission, symlink confinement and immutable content verification remain unchanged.
6. Installation/report status distinguishes failure before commit from cleanup failure after a committed activation when relevant; it must not imply old selection was preserved when it was changed.

## Deduplication and prioritization

Live all-state activation+SDK search returned only unrelated #8286. #8228 is a Linux delivery umbrella, including historical rollback goals, not a current implementation fix for this split-pointer path. #8281 and first-pass BUILD-01 concern cache identities; #8283 concerns CI execution and retention. This is a narrow installer follow-on, not a replacement package manager or new remote registry/signature system. P2 is appropriate for interruption/failure recovery; it is not a P1 successful-install corruption claim.

No issue was published. The exact installer tests are retained in `evidence/test_toolchain_install.py`; archive resumption tests are retained in `evidence/test_linux_sdk_publication.py`.

items.title: [Enhancement] Reduce Docker image size
items.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
The current Docker image size is around 120 MB because it is based on Debian. For a self-hosted project, especially one written in Go, this image size is unnecessarily large. Go compiles into a single static binary, meaning it does not require a heavy Debian userland, package manager, or standard libraries to run. Large images consume extra disk space, increase bandwidth usage during updates, and prolong deployment times for users with limited server resources.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to request an optimization of the distribution size. A great solution would be switching the base image from Debian to a lighter alternative, such as Alpine Linux (which would reduce the base to ~10-50 MB) or, ideally, using a multi-stage Docker build with a scratch or distroless image. This would allow the final production image to contain only the compiled Go binary and essential assets.

**Why would you like this feature to be added?**
Optimizing the image size brings several key benefits:

* Resource Efficiency: Self-hosted users often run projects on low-spec hardware like Raspberry Pis or cheap VPS instances where disk space and RAM are limited.
* Faster Deployments: Smaller images mean much faster download and startup times during updates.
* Enhanced Security: Switching to Alpine, distroless, or scratch drastically reduces the attack surface by removing unused tools, shells, and packages, minimizing potential CVE vulnerabilities.

Thanks.

### Subsystem

build / ci (TypeScript, Rust, WASM, bundling)

### Priority

P2

### Defect

On PR #5790, push run 40683872711 at head fe7fe671aa55772f97c8811c24271e084591c175 failed in the Lint job (122802661004) during Set up pnpm, before dependency installation or lint. The pinned pnpm/action-setup commit 0977fd99725f1db4007ccb2928dbb4e90d06cc86 bootstrapped pnpm 11.19.0, then tried to switch to the project-pinned pnpm 11.6.0. Its verifier reported ERR_PNPM_PNPM_ENGINE_IDENTITY_UNVERIFIABLE for @pnpm/linux-x64@11.6.0 because the operation timed out. The log proves a transport timeout, not corrupted bytes, an invalid signature, or a malicious registry; the generic tampering sentence is emitted for unreachable metadata too.

Source inspection shows the 11.19 bootstrap verifies both package-manager wrappers and the host platform package even when selecting the JavaScript engine. pnpm 11.6.0 uses that JavaScript engine without the Linux native wrapper. pnpm 11.26.0 narrows verification to the selected engine and platform packages it actually uses, while retaining signature checks. The pinned action bootstraps 11.19.0; published action-setup v6.1.0 still bootstraps 11.25.0. No reviewed immutable action commit containing the 11.26.0 fix is available yet, so a simple action-version bump is not a fix. Keep the project target at 11.6.0 and all signature, TLS, and integrity checks enabled. This is shared validation infrastructure; coordinate with its current workflow owners before changing its action pin.

### Reproduce

Original evidence: inspect PR #5790 push run 40683872711, head fe7fe671aa55772f97c8811c24271e084591c175, Lint job 122802661004. It failed in pnpm/action-setup while switching 11.19.0 to 11.6.0; Set up Node, dependency install, and lint were never reached. Preserve this failed run; do not rerun it.

Before adopting an immutable action-setup pin carrying the selected-engine fix, prove with controlled fixtures that a timeout from the unused @pnpm/linux-x64 metadata endpoint no longer blocks JavaScript pnpm 11.6.0, and that the exact JavaScript package is still signature/integrity verified. A timeout, missing/bad signature, or altered integrity for the executing JavaScript package must fail closed; selecting a native engine must still verify its required platform package. Verify no target activation on failure and actual pnpm 11.6.0 activation on success. Then run fresh required validation on the changed exact head and confirm lint executes. Do not disable verification, change the project pnpm target, increase timeouts speculatively, or use a retry/empty commit to relabel the original failure green.

### References

Workflow: .github/workflows/validation.yml, lint job Set up pnpm step (currently pinned to pnpm/action-setup@0977fd99725f1db4007ccb2928dbb4e90d06cc86).
PR/run evidence: https://github.com/jcosta33/sourdaw/pull/5790 and https://github.com/jcosta33/sourdaw/actions/runs/40683872711/job/122802661004
Upstream code fix: pnpm 11.26.0 selected-engine verification, https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/blob/v11.26.0/pnpm11/engine/pm/commands/src/self-updater/verifyPnpmEngineIdentity.ts ; release https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/releases/tag/v11.26.0.
Current action bootstrap evidence: https://github.com/pnpm/action-setup/blob/v6.1.0/src/install-pnpm/bootstrap/pnpm-lock.json. No action pin carrying the fix has been established.


### Selected-engine repair delivered

[PR #5911](https://github.com/jcosta33/sourdaw/pull/5911) merged on main as [f8b65fd1cc](https://github.com/jcosta33/sourdaw/commit/f8b65fd1ccad56a08a7ad4b33ef68a71e3d6206f). The reviewed 11.26.0 bootstrap verifies the selected JavaScript pnpm 11.6.0 before exports; source-manifest leaf and ancestor redirects refuse before acquisition. The project target, canonical registry, TLS, signature and integrity requirements remain intact.

Controlled fixtures executed real upstream pnpm verification, ECDSA and tarball-integrity paths. With identical resolved locks and an explicit Linux collector-helper input, 11.19 refused solely on the unused Linux verification endpoint, while 11.26 avoided that lookup and activated authenticated JavaScript 11.6.0. Executing-package timeout, absent/bad signature, altered integrity and corrupt tarball refused activation; selecting a native engine retained required platform verification. These fixtures physically ran on macOS: they are a controlled Linux-endpoint witness, not a replay of the original Linux network incident. Normal Linux and native-platform integration is separate CI evidence.

The first admitted [Health run 41068988140](https://github.com/jcosta33/sourdaw/actions/runs/41068988140) on exact head 82949fb7191cb69354e7dea317e915ede92dafcb passed required Gate, HeavyGate, all twelve browser shards, WebGPU admission, four unit shards and selected build, lint, type and native validation. Review tooling was scope-skipped. Lint executed after verified pnpm activation. Independent current-head review and repaired/confirmed manifest-authority findings preceded native delivery.

The original #5790 failure remains preserved without rerun. Its own lane must now integrate the actual landed fix and obtain fresh changed-head validation and review before that PR can deliver; this repair does not discharge unrelated saved-project reload failures or campaign acceptance.
